title: Global Debt
subtitle: More than 300% of world GDP
subject: comprendreLeMonde
description: World debt has never been higher. Should we worry about it, or is it a normal tool for funding growth and getting through crises?

hero.hook: Japan owes the equivalent of 260% of its GDP... and nobody is worried. Here is why.

blocks.text: World debt, that of states, companies and households combined, now goes beyond **300% of world GDP**, an absolute record in economic history.
That impressive figure hides a more subtle reality. Debt pays for growth, for the answer to health crises, and for the green transition. But it also carries the risk that confidence collapses.

sections.title: How a state goes into debt

blocks.text: A state goes into debt when its spending is structurally higher than its tax revenue. That budget deficit is filled by borrowing on the financial markets. According to [[Keynesian theory]], borrowing to stimulate the economy during a crisis is legitimate, as long as the money is paid back once growth returns.

In practice, governments borrow easily in hard times but rarely repay in good ones, so debt piles up for good. Japan is a fascinating case. With debt close to 260% of its GDP, the country should logically be in crisis. It is not, because most of that debt is held by its own banks and savers, out of reach of foreign markets.
It was only in 2015 that the United Kingdom finished repaying debts dating from the Napoleonic wars and from a financial bubble of 1720.
The real danger of a debt depends not only on its size, but on the currency it is borrowed in. Rich countries borrow in their own currency, which reassures investors.

blocks.caption: World public debt now tops 300% of the planet's GDP

blocks.text: Developing countries often have to borrow in dollars, for want of a currency seen as stable enough. If their national currency loses value against the dollar, the sum they owe explodes overnight. In these crises the [[IMF]] often steps in, but it usually imposes strict austerity policies that weigh heavily on the population.

Two visions of the economy clash here. [[Modern Monetary Theory]] holds that a state cannot go bankrupt as long as it borrows in its own currency: the real limit is not an arbitrary figure, like the 60% set by the Maastricht Treaty in Europe, but the level of inflation.

More cautious economists fear that too much debt will scare the markets away and send interest rates sharply higher. The euro zone crisis of 2010 to 2012 showed that risk. Countries like Greece, with no central bank of their own, saw their borrowing rates soar until they threatened the very existence of the European currency.

World debt is not only about states. Companies and households carry a growing share of it too, sometimes through lightly regulated financial players. A new debate is opening around climate debt: should borrowing that funds the energy transition be treated differently from borrowing that funds ordinary consumption?

Fairness between generations remains a central question, because borrowing today means drawing on tomorrow's taxes. But if that money pays for lasting infrastructure or a good education, it can also be seen as a gift passed on to future generations rather than a burden.

World debt has passed 300% of the planet's GDP, a historic record. How dangerous it is depends less on its size than on the currency it is borrowed in: Japan proves that a debt of 260% can stay stable when it is held at home.
